item.description:

  • Prior 52.5

  • Prior 53.4

Key findings:

  • German Composite PMI climbs to highest since March 2022

Comment:

Phil Smith, Economics Associate Director at S&P Global Market Intelligence said

"The slowdown in growth at the start of the fourth quarter proved short-lived, with November's provisional PMI results showing the Composite Output Index resume its recent ascent and move to its highest since March 2022. "Encouragingly, alongside the sustained upturn in manufacturing, which continues to see support from rising export orders, demand also revived in the more domestic-oriented service sector and showed the strongest improvement in more than a year, hinting at a broadening recovery. "Labour market conditions remain subdued, although it's notable that manufacturing employment has returned to growth amid increasing pressure on factory capacity and an improvement in business expectations, ending the longest sequence of manufacturing job cuts in the survey's history and perhaps signalling growing confidence among goods producers in the durability of the recovery."

Manufacturing remained the main growth driver, with output expanding at its fastest pace in over five years, while services activity also reached a one-year high. Underlying demand improved significantly, with new orders rising at the fastest pace in more than four and a half years, supported by stronger domestic demand and export sales. Manufacturing employment returned to growth for the first time in nearly three and a half years, although overall employment declined slightly due to continued job cuts in services.

Business confidence improved to a nine-month high, driven by stronger optimism among manufacturers, whose expectations reached their highest level since February. Services firms, however, became less optimistic and continued to reduce staffing levels. On the inflation front, input cost pressures remained historically elevated but eased to a three-month low, while output price inflation accelerated slightly, mainly reflecting more aggressive price increases in the services sector.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

Comment:

Joe Hayes, Senior Principal Economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence said

"The November 'flash' PMI data have raised the odds of France entering a technical recession in the fourth quarter. The eurozone's second-largest economy is struggling with weak domestic demand, in part due to hesitancy from clients to commit to projects ahead of a highly uncertain election period next year. "We've subsequently seen a rapid deterioration in business confidence these past few months as other long-standing issues, such as concerns about France's fiscal position, resurface as the election draws closer. The survey's sentiment measure, the Future Activity Index, sank to its lowest level since late 2012 in November, if we exclude pandemic-impacted months. "It's also notable that output price inflation has slowed sharply in November. This suggests that company pricing power has diminished and further highlights the fragility of the French economy."

France’s private sector activity contracted at its fastest pace since May in November. Manufacturing led the downturn, with factory output declining at its sharpest pace since February 2025, while services activity also weakened. New orders fell markedly amid weak domestic demand, economic uncertainty, competition and cost pressures. Backlogs declined at the fastest pace since August, prompting companies to reduce staffing levels for a seventh consecutive month.

Looking ahead, business confidence deteriorated sharply, with firms reporting their most pessimistic 12-month outlook since October 2012, excluding the initial COVID-19 lockdown period. Meanwhile, input cost inflation remained elevated but eased to a three-month low, while output price inflation slowed to an eight-month low as companies faced greater competitive pressures and resistance to price increases. Overall, the survey points to worsening economic momentum alongside some easing of inflationary pressures.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

What are FX option expiries?

The FX option expiration price levels refer to the strike prices where option contracts are set to expire. These levels include both calls and puts.

When you see "EUR/USD at 1.1600 for €4 billion" it means there is a total of €4 billion worth of options (calls + puts combined) that have a strike price of 1.1600 and are expiring at that specific time (the "New York Cut" at 10:00 AM ET).

Traders watch these levels because they often act as a "magnet" for the price. For example, if there's nothing happening in the market and the price is close to the expiry level, let's say 30-50 pips away, what you will usually see is the price moving into the expiry level. This happens due to the hedging activity of the market makers (banks, dealers and so on).

As the price gets closer to the strike price near expiration, these market makers must aggressively buy or sell the currency to hedge their risk. This hedging activity tends to suppress volatility and keep the price "pinned" close to the strike price until the expiration time passes.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: Nasdaq analysis today as we wake up to the green
item.description:
Nasdaq futures jump more than 3% after tech rout. Can buyers turn the rebound into a recovery?

Nasdaq 100 futures are staging a powerful comeback on Monday, November 23, following last week's technology selloff. The short-term picture has improved, but the market is approaching a price area that could determine whether the rebound gains momentum or meets renewed selling.

Nasdaq 100 E-mini futures (December 2026 contract) were trading at 25,928.50, up 802 points or 3.19%, in the early Monday European morning snapshot.

The rally follows a bruising week for technology stocks, when concerns about AI valuations, financing and investment returns contributed to heavy selling across US equities.

But after last week's brutal stretch for risk assets, traders are waking up to a tentative breather, with Eamonn Sheridan at investingLive.com noting that US stock futures jumped over 2% in a relief bounce alongside a spot gold rally toward $3,620, pushing S&P 500 futures near 7,090 and Nasdaq 100 futures around 25,830 as margin-call pressure eased, even while Seoul's Kospi slid nearly 4% to 4,680 in holiday-thinned Asian trade.

Offering a constructive counter-narrative to last week's hawkish repricing, Eamonn also detailed how JPMorgan's David Kelly views the tech correction as overdue and expects stocks to bounce on steady 401(k) inflows and corporate buybacks, projecting a single December Fed hike followed by a pause as lower gasoline prices shave roughly 0.4 points off November's annual CPI.

Still, upside follow-through in the broader AI trade faces a stubborn legal overhang after California widened its Nvidia investigation to potential criminal violations over China chip sales, adding state-level subpoena and disclosure risk on top of an active SEC inquiry and complicating market speculation over a quick Jensen Huang return.

Back to Nasdaq futures today, so far, there is a meaningful improvement in the shorter-term price structure. Buyers have recovered ground lost during Friday's selloff and are now challenging the upper boundary of the overnight trading range.

But a 3% rally following a particularly severe decline is not automatically a trend reversal. The next reactions around resistance and support should give traders a clearer picture.

The 25,934-25,945 area is the first obstacle

The overnight recovery has already encountered resistance around 25,945, with an additional technical reference near 25,934-25,936.

Interestingly, price has approached the upper boundary more than once without establishing a sustained breakout.

Holding above this area would strengthen the bullish case and potentially open a path toward 26,000, followed by a higher chart reference near 26,253.

Repeated rejection, however, could encourage profit-taking and give short sellers another opportunity.

Also, 26399 is the Nasdaq futures (NQ) year 2025 high (that held for 23 weeks till mid April 2026). That may be a price magnet for this week. A price magnet is a price level or zone that tends to attract market activity or special market participants attention, often because of concentrated liquidity, trading volume, or pending orders, although there is no guarantee that price will reach it.

The buying is improving, but there is a nuance

The order-flow data reveal something worth examining.

Despite the considerable recovery in price, cumulative volume delta was only moderately positive, around +1,827 contracts against approximately 116,585 contracts traded during the developing overnight session.

This suggests that the price recovery has been much larger than the net imbalance between aggressive buying and selling.

It is consistent with reduced selling pressure and potentially short covering, rather than necessarily requiring overwhelming aggressive buying. It does not establish which participants drove the advance.

The positive development is that buyers are achieving meaningful price progress. The unanswered question is whether that progress can survive renewed selling.

Nasdaq support levels if the rally pulls back

25,850: An important overnight high-volume area. Holding around this level on a pullback would be constructive.

25,747: Near the lower boundary of the overnight value area. Losing this area would weaken the immediate recovery structure.

25,611: A previous overnight reaction low. A move back toward this level would indicate that sellers have recovered considerably more ground.

For broader perspective, Friday's low around 24,977 remains a reference for the preceding selloff.

The outlook for Monday's US session

The short-term outlook has improved, but the US cash-market opening will provide another test as regular-session trading begins.

A sustained move beyond 25,945, particularly if followed by buyers defending that level on a pullback, would be encouraging.

Alternatively, another rejection followed by a loss of 25,850 would suggest that the market needs more time to establish support.

The distinction is between a powerful rebound and a sustainable recovery. Nasdaq futures have demonstrated the first. The second still needs evidence.

Anthropic stock: Can $87.80 become a foundation for recovery?

Remember that we have a new darling on the AI block and people are watching. Anthropic (ANT) shares fell 8.50% on Friday, closing at $88.91, but recovered to approximately $91.78 in overnight trading on Monday, November 23, up 3.67% from Friday's close. One particularly interesting reference is $87.80, approximately Friday's volume-weighted average price (VWAP). This represents the average price paid during Friday's session, weighted by trading volume. Despite the heavy selloff, the stock finished above that reference, which makes it worth monitoring as a potential support level.

My short-term interpretation is bullish as long as Anthropic holds above approximately $87.80, with an important qualification: holding above support is constructive, but it does not guarantee a recovery. A sustained move above $90-$91 could improve the picture further, while a return below $87.80 would weaken the bullish argument and put Friday's $83.05 low back into focus. For traders, the more revealing test may be how shares react if they revisit $87.80, rather than simply how much they gain during overnight trading.

This article was written by Itai Levitan at investinglive.com.

Summary:

  • S&P 500 futures rose about 2.2% and Nasdaq 100 futures close to 3%, holding near session highs after last week's rout.
  • The Kospi fell almost 6% at its low, triggering a sidecar on program selling, before paring losses to around 3.2%. Shanghai fell about 1% and the Hang Seng about 0.7%. Japan was closed.
  • The Fed debate intensified: Bessent warned against overtightening, Ackman urged a 3% inflation target, and JPMorgan's Kelly expects one hike then a pause.

  • Gold rose about 2% to near $3,610 as forced selling eased. Brent held near $90.
  • The dollar eased against most majors but USD/JPY rose to near 159. NZ retail sales beat forecasts, and Australia's flash PMI hit a five-year low.

Relief rally holds through Asia

US equity index futures kept most of their early rebound through the Asian session on Monday, offering a pause after Wall Street's worst week in years. S&P 500 futures were up around 2.2% near 7,090, and Nasdaq 100 futures gained close to 3% to around 25,870, both trading near their session highs. The tone was one of relief, not recovery, with the AI valuation debate unresolved and the Federal Reserve's 9 December decision still ahead.

Seoul trips a sidecar, then steadies

Korean stocks bore the brunt of the early selling. The Kospi fell almost 6% at its low, near 4,590, prompting the Korea Exchange to trigger a sidecar, a temporary halt on program selling designed to slow sharp falls. The index then recovered to trade down around 3.2% near 4,710. Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix were each down about 3.6%.

The rebound followed a weekend emergency meeting at which Korean officials began preparing a market stabilisation fund of about 10.8 trillion won, roughly $8 billion. If deployed, it would be the fund's first use since 2008. Authorities also eased daily share buyback limits for three months and launched a crackdown on illegal short selling, though they stopped short of a short-selling ban. The Bank of Korea meets on Thursday, and economists expect another quarter-point rate hike.

China cuts margin requirements, brokers call a bottom

Mainland China's Shanghai Composite fell about 1%, and Hong Kong's Hang Seng lost about 0.7% after recovering from earlier lows. Over the weekend, China's three exchanges cut the minimum margin requirement for buying stocks on credit to 80% from 100%, effective 30 November, and announced fee cuts and plans for market makers on the ChiNext board. CITIC Securities and China Securities both struck a constructive tone, with CITIC seeing a broader rally next year. Many large Chinese brokerages are state-controlled, and their supportive calls tend to echo the official policy push. Japanese markets were closed for a public holiday.

The Fed debate gets louder

Pressure on the Fed to slow its tightening built through the session. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said many believe the Fed may be making a policy mistake if it overtightens, citing a sharp tightening in financial conditions. Pershing Square's Bill Ackman went further, arguing the Fed should replace its 2% inflation target with 3% and warning that more hikes risk recession. JPMorgan Asset Management's David Kelly said he expects one hike in December followed by a pause, describing Governor Christopher Waller as largely alone in backing a 50 basis point move.

The other side remains well represented. Waller has said the Fed should hike by 50 basis points or signal a January follow-up, Goldman Sachs economists expect hikes in December and March, and futures price a December move as close to certain. OCBC strategists said the rate shock may have become a growth shock, with dollar strength now falling mainly on emerging market currencies.

Nvidia: politics versus process

President Donald Trump posted that he hopes Nvidia's board rehires Jensen Huang, calling it the best outcome for the company and the country. Bessent has also softened his stance, saying any return depends on what investigators find. The legal picture is moving the other way. California's attorney general said his investigation into whether Nvidia or Huang misled the public over chip sales to China now covers potential criminal violations of state law, and the SEC is also investigating. The board has said it does not intend to reinstate Huang.

Gold rebounds, oil steady

Gold rose about 2% to near $3,610 an ounce, and silver gained around 2.2%, as the forced selling that drove last week's slide eased. Brent edged up to around $90 a barrel and WTI to near $83.60. Goldman Sachs expects Brent to fall to $78 by the end of 2027 as the market moves into surplus, and sees European gas prices roughly halving next year.

FX: dollar softer, yen weaker

The US dollar eased against most majors. AUD/USD rose about 0.3% to near 0.6640, and EUR/USD was near 1.0980. NZD/USD was flat near 0.5470. The yen was the exception, with USD/JPY up about 0.3% to near 159 in holiday-thinned trade. The US 10-year Treasury yield rose about 3 basis points to near 4.94% as haven demand faded.

Data and central banks

New Zealand third-quarter retail sales volumes jumped 2.2%, far above the 0.5% forecast. Australia's flash composite PMI fell to 46.1, its lowest since August 2021, though price pressures eased. Swiss National Bank Vice Chairman Antoine Martin said the bank is watching closely for second-round inflation effects ahead of its December decision.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Crypto crime: Fusionist's ACE bridge emptied of $3.7 million as traders follow a $2 million exploit
item.description:
ACE fell to about $0.0001 on BNB Chain but still traded around $0.04 on centralised exchanges, and traders exploited that gap until the bridge ran dry. The drained 53.7 million tokens are almost half of the roughly 116 million ACE in circulation before the attack. They now sit in 24 wallets, and one wallet alone holds 26.1 million, so the main near-term risk is selling pressure on exchange-listed ACE. Gate is moving its ACE perpetuals to reduce-only and then delisting them, which leaves one fewer place to hedge. The incident is too small to affect BTC, ETH, crypto equities or ETF flows. Its main significance is for how the market prices bridge risk in small-cap gaming tokens.

---

One abused minter role let a hacker walk off with $2 million, and a crowd of opportunists took the next $3.7 million before the bridge ran out of tokens.

Summary:

  • On Sunday an attacker used privileged minter access on Fusionist's bridge to create unbacked ACE on BNB Chain, starting with 3.5 million tokens and finishing with a single mint of 10 quintillion.
  • The tokens were sold as they were minted for about 1,150 ETH, roughly $2 million. The proceeds were moved to Ethereum and sent into Tornado Cash.
  • Traders bought the cheap BNB Chain ACE and redeemed it through the bridge, taking about 53.7 million real ACE (about $3.7 million) across 24 addresses and leaving 0.08 ACE behind.
  • One wallet turned about $50 into roughly $17,670 in under 20 minutes. Another 27 redemptions, totalling 1.36 billion tokens, failed because the bridge had run out of tokens.
  • Fusionist paused ACE transfers, trading and bridging on BNB Chain. Gate is reversing ACE/USDT trades made during the exploit and will delist its ACE perpetuals.

An attacker exploited privileged minting access on blockchain gaming studio Fusionist's ACE bridge on Sunday, creating vast amounts of unbacked ACE on BNB Chain and selling them for about $2 million, according to an analysis of onchain data by The Block. Opportunistic traders then bought the near-worthless copies and redeemed them through the bridge for genuine tokens, stripping it of about 53.7 million ACE worth roughly $3.7 million.

ACE is the native token of Endurance, the blockchain Fusionist runs to support its sci-fi strategy games, and it pays transaction fees on that network. A version of the token also lives on BNB Chain. The bridge between the two normally holds Endurance ACE as backing, so burning a BNB Chain token releases an equal amount on Endurance. That design held only as long as nobody could mint BNB Chain ACE without collateral.

Onchain Lens said the attacker abused the bridge's minter role, and The Block found the mints came from a wallet funded by Fusionist's deployer almost three years ago. Security firm Blockaid, which first flagged the exploit, listed that wallet among the attacker's addresses. The minting began just before 1 p.m. US Eastern time with 3.5 million tokens and escalated over roughly two and a half hours, ending with a single mint of 10 quintillion ACE. Each batch was dumped into decentralised exchange pools as soon as it appeared, and the proceeds of about 1,150 ETH were moved to Ethereum and routed into the Tornado Cash mixer.

The selling drove BNB Chain ACE to about $0.0001 while the token still fetched around $0.04 on centralised exchanges, and that gap is where the second loss came from. The Block traced one wallet that started with about $50, spent $10 testing the bridge and used the remaining $40 to buy roughly 404,000 ACE. The bridge released the same number of real tokens within minutes, and the trader sold them for about $17,670, a return of around 350 times, all in under 20 minutes.

By Sunday afternoon the bridge held 0.08 ACE, and a further 27 redemption attempts totalling about 1.36 billion tokens failed for lack of reserves. Fusionist told users to pause ACE transfers, trading and bridging on BNB Chain while it investigated, but had issued no further update at the time of The Block's report. Gate said it would reverse all ACE/USDT trades from the first mint to 2:15 p.m. Eastern, leaving some sellers with negative balances, and moved its ACE perpetual futures to reduce-only ahead of a planned delisting.

The incident adds to a long run of bridge failures in 2026 and shows how one compromised privilege can turn a contained theft into a public scramble. How Fusionist handles the tokens now sitting with the traders who drained it, and whether other exchanges follow Gate in unwinding trades, are the next questions for ACE holders. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: California widens Nvidia probe to criminal law, a bigger deal than Huang return talk
item.description:
An open-ended state criminal investigation, on top of an SEC probe, adds a legal risk premium that's hard to price. That could cap Nvidia rebounds even as the broader market steadies. The stock's weight in major indices means headline risk here can spill into the Nasdaq and the wider AI trade, and into Asian chip names already under pressure. Investors may also start pricing a lower chance of Huang returning, which removes one potential upside catalyst that some had been counting on. The board's subpoena response and any disclosure in regulatory filings are the near-term flashpoints.

Newswire cut: California's Nvidia probe now covers possible criminal breaches of state law over China chip sales and whether Nvidia or ex-CEO Jensen Huang misled the public, AG Rob Bonta said. The SEC is also investigating, raising the stakes for any Huang return.

One-line wrap: The market has been arguing about whether Huang comes back, while California has been quietly building a case that could make that question irrelevant.

Summary:

  • California AG Rob Bonta says his Nvidia investigation covers potential criminal violations of state law.
  • The probe examines whether Nvidia or Huang gave false information about chip sales to China, and whether investors were misled. It is preliminary, with no conclusions.
  • Bonta served Nvidia with an investigative subpoena on 19 November, a week after Huang resigned.
  • The SEC is also investigating, reportedly including whether Nvidia misled investors.
  • The criminal angle makes a quick Huang return harder to justify, despite support from Trump and a softer stance from Bessent.

California's investigation into Nvidia has widened to include possible criminal violations of state law. It's a significant escalation that has drawn less attention than the debate over whether former chief executive Jensen Huang could return to run the company.

State Attorney General Rob Bonta said on Friday that a range of California laws could have been broken if Nvidia or Huang gave false information to the public about sales of advanced chips to China. He stressed that the inquiry is at a preliminary stage and has not reached any conclusions.

Bonta opened the probe a day earlier, serving Nvidia with an investigative subpoena. His office is examining whether the company's or Huang's actions allowed China to obtain advanced chips or confidential information, and whether Nvidia misled investors and the public about that risk. Because Nvidia is headquartered in Santa Clara, the state has jurisdiction to pursue possible breaches of its own laws. The investigation follows Huang's resignation earlier this month after reports of an affair with a woman US officials suspect of spying for China. She was linked to Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company under scrutiny for possibly diverting restricted Nvidia chips. The Securities and Exchange Commission is also investigating, and its inquiry is reported to include whether Nvidia misled investors.

The criminal angle matters more than recent headlines suggest. Over the past week, much of the market conversation has centred on whether Huang might come back. President Donald Trump has backed his return, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent no longer rules it out, and activist investor Bill Ackman has floated a shareholder route to reinstate him. That focus risks playing down the legal exposure now building at state and federal level. A state criminal probe that explicitly covers statements by Huang himself makes any quick reinstatement much harder for the board to justify, whatever the investor pressure. It also leaves Nvidia facing open-ended legal and disclosure risk at a time when its shares are already under heavy pressure.

The probes also highlight a split in approach: Washington's messaging on Huang has softened, while California is widening the scope of its inquiry.

For investors, the next markers are Nvidia's response to the subpoena, any detail on the scope of the SEC's investigation, and the company's answers on export compliance to federal officials, whose 10-day request expires this week.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: OCBC: AI rout becomes a growth shock as EM currencies take the dollar's strength
item.description:
If OCBC is right, dollar strength will be most visible in high-yielding and externally exposed EM currencies. That makes the case for selective EM FX hedges even while the dollar softens against the majors. Carry trades funded in low-yielders are vulnerable to further unwinding if the AI sell-off resumes, which could add volatility to Asian currencies, especially those tied to chip exports. A clearer Fed pause signal, along the lines JPMorgan's Kelly expects, would be the main thing that could ease the pressure on EM. Any repeat of last week's forced selling in metals would support the "growth shock" reading.

- The AI unwind has stopped being just a rates story, OCBC says, and emerging market currencies are paying for the dollar's resilience.

Summary:

  • OCBC strategists say the interest rate shock may have evolved into a growth shock, as AI de-risking hits equities, EM carry trades and metals.
  • Concerns over the AI investment cycle have lowered stocks and US yields, shifting the pressure from the stronger dollar onto EM currencies.
  • They expect the dollar to stay supported in the short term by hawkish Fed risk and tightening global financial conditions.
  • In October, OCBC's Sim Moh Siong and Christopher Wong warned that a US-centric AI shock could hurt the dollar. By November they expected it to stay firm into 1H27.
  • The "growth shock" framing echoes Goldman Sachs' view that the sell-off has broadened beyond an AI unwind.

The market shock driven by higher interest rates may have turned into a growth shock, according to OCBC Bank strategists. They said the unwinding of AI-related risk is now hitting equities, emerging market carry trades and metals at the same time.

In a report on Monday, the strategists said worries about the AI investment cycle have pushed down both stocks and US Treasury yields. As a result, the pressure from a strong US dollar has shifted onto emerging market currencies, not spread across the major currencies. In the near term, they expect the dollar to keep benefiting from the risk of a more hawkish Federal Reserve and from the strain that tighter global financial conditions put on the rest of the world.

The view marks a notable evolution for the Singapore bank. In mid-October, OCBC FX strategists Sim Moh Siong and Christopher Wong described AI as the dollar's potential weak spot. They argued that when a shock starts in the US, losses on US assets can outweigh the currency's usual safe-haven appeal. By early November they had turned more supportive, expecting the dollar to stay firm into the first half of 2027, with EUR/USD potentially dipping below 1.10 before recovering later in the year. At the time, they also cautioned that markets might start to question how far the Fed could tighten if AI-related stress led to a sharp tightening in financial conditions.

Monday's note suggests both forces are now in play. Financial conditions have tightened sharply: US equities had their worst week in years, and Goldman Sachs measured its biggest weekly tightening since March 2020. Yet the dollar's strength is showing up mainly against emerging market currencies, which are more exposed to capital outflows and funding stress. Korea illustrates the dynamic: the Kospi has come under heavy pressure and authorities have readied a market stabilisation fund.

The framing echoes Goldman Sachs strategist Ben Snider, who said last week that the sell-off had expanded from an AI unwind into a broader growth downgrade.

In early Asian trade on Monday, the dollar eased against major currencies as US stock futures bounced. OCBC's warning is that the relief may be uneven: as long as the Fed keeps its tightening bias and global conditions stay tight, emerging market currencies are likely to remain the pressure point. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: JPMorgan's Kelly: tech correction overdue, stocks to bounce, Fed to hike once then pause
item.description:

If December's statement or projections lean his way, front-end yields and the dollar could ease. Waller's push for 50bp, or a clear signal of a January follow-up, remains the main risk to that view. November CPI is now a key data point: a sizeable gasoline-driven drop would strengthen the case for a pause. Kelly's flow argument (401(k)s, buybacks, wealthy buyers) suggests dips may keep attracting support, even if the AI valuation debate isn't settled.

Kelly sees a healthy tech shakeout, a cooling economy outside AI and a Fed that hikes once and stops, a much gentler script than the one markets traded last week.

Summary:

  • JPMorgan Asset Management's David Kelly says a tech correction was overdue, driven by Nvidia's problems and wider disruption.
  • He sees little strong demand outside tech and expects falling gasoline prices to cut about 0.4 points from November's annual CPI rate.
  • He expects a December Fed hike followed by a pause, and says Waller is largely alone in backing 50bp.
  • Waller has said the Fed should hike 50bp in December or signal a January follow-up. Dallas Fed President Logan has also shown openness to faster tightening.
  • Kelly expects steady inflows from 401(k)s, buybacks and wealthy investors to help the market bounce.

The stock market was due a correction in technology shares and is likely to bounce back, according to David Kelly, chief global strategist at JPMorgan Asset Management. He also pushed back against expectations of aggressive Federal Reserve tightening.

In an interview with CNBC late last week, Kelly said the pullback had been driven by Nvidia's recent problems and wider technological disruption, which he acknowledged were unsettling some investors. Outside the technology sector, though, he saw little evidence of strong demand, pointing to flat new housing activity and weak spending on consumer basics. He also expects inflation pressure to ease. He estimated that falling gasoline prices alone will take around four-tenths of a percentage point off the annual rate of consumer price inflation in November.

On policy, Kelly expects the Fed to raise rates in December and then pause, not keep tightening. He described Governor Christopher Waller as a lonely voice in backing a 50 basis point hike, and said he doesn't believe most policymakers share that view. He argued that markets were building a hawkish story in the absence of clear forward guidance, and that with rates already close to neutral there's no reason for the Fed to be aggressive.

Waller's position has hardened over the past fortnight. In a speech in London on 10 November, he said he was leaning toward a quarter-point increase in December but would consider half a point if inflation ran hot, warning that a smaller move could put the Fed's credibility at risk. After October's consumer price data came in above forecasts, he told CNBC on 18 November that the Fed should either raise rates by 50 basis points at its 8 to 9 December meeting or clearly signal another increase in January. Waller isn't entirely alone, either: Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan also signalled openness to a faster pace earlier this month.

Kelly is still upbeat on the market's resilience. He pointed to steady inflows from 401(k) retirement contributions, corporate buybacks and purchases by wealthy Americans as a consistent source of support. He said that unless there is a major reason for negativity, the market is likely to recover.

His view is at the softer end of the range. Goldman Sachs economists expect hikes in both December and March, and futures price a December move as close to certain. The size of that move, and any signal on what comes next, will be the key tests for Kelly's one-and-done call. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Ackman urges Fed to drop 2% inflation goal for 3%, warns 9 December hike risks recession
item.description:
Ackman's post adds to a growing chorus, now including the Treasury, arguing against further Fed hikes. That could feed hopes of a softer message on 9 December even if the hike itself goes ahead. Rate markets are unlikely to shift much on investor commentary alone. Any sign that Fed officials are open to slowing the pace, though, would weigh on the dollar and front-end yields and support equities and gold. His SpaceX example also points to strain in credit markets, so corporate bond spreads are worth watching as a gauge of how much tightening is already in the system.

---

---

Ackman wants the Fed to move the goalposts to 3%, but a central bank that changes its target mid-fight risks losing the credibility it needs to win it.

Summary:

  • Pershing Square CEO Bill Ackman says the Fed is set to make a mistake at its 9 December meeting.
  • He says financial conditions have tightened massively, citing SpaceX's secured debt at around 8.3% against below 6% for its IPO-era unsecured bonds, plus a higher cost of equity after the sell-off.
  • He argues 2% is unrealistic given geopolitics, defence spending, deglobalisation, tariffs and AI-related investment, and that 3% is more realistic.
  • He warns that more hikes aimed at reaching 2% would push the US and the world into recession.
  • His view echoes Treasury Secretary Bessent's warning against overtightening, though futures still price a December hike as near-certain.

Pershing Square chief executive Bill Ackman has called on the Federal Reserve to abandon its 2% inflation target in favour of 3%. He warned that the central bank is about to make another mistake at its 9 December meeting and risks pushing the US and global economies into recession if it keeps raising rates.

In a post on X, Ackman argued that financial conditions have already tightened sharply. He pointed to SpaceX, which he described as an investment-grade company, raising secured debt at an interest rate of around 8.3%, compared with below 6% on the unsecured bonds it sold at the time of its listing. He added that the recent slide in the stock market has also made equity capital materially more expensive.

His broader case is that the world has changed since the 2% goal was set. Ackman cited geopolitical risk and the need for higher global military spending, deglobalisation and tariffs, and the vast investment under way in AI infrastructure and the energy needed to power it. Against that backdrop, he said, "3% inflation is a more realistic ambition in the new world." He ended the post by inviting critics to tell him why he was wrong.

The intervention comes in a week of growing pushback against further tightening. On Sunday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned that the Fed risks a policy mistake if it overtightens. Goldman Sachs data also show US financial conditions recorded their sharpest weekly tightening since March 2020 after last week's equity rout. Even so, futures price a December hike as close to certain, and Goldman's own economists expect increases in December and March.

The counterargument is likely to centre on credibility. Raising the target while inflation is running above it could be seen as moving the goalposts. That risks loosening the long-term inflation expectations the Fed has spent decades anchoring, and could mean higher rates later, not lower ones. Policymakers have so far leaned the other way: Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson said last week that rates will need to rise again because inflation is too high.

With the 9 December decision approaching, the debate over how much tightening the economy can take, and what the Fed should be aiming for, is now playing out openly between policymakers, the Treasury and some of Wall Street's most prominent investors. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: US stock futures jump over 2% in relief bounce, gold rallies, but Kospi slides nearly 4%
item.description:
The bounce looks driven by positioning and policy headlines, not by any change in the AI valuation debate. Rallies could fade quickly if cash markets in New York don't confirm the futures move. Gold rising alongside stocks suggests margin-call selling has paused, which makes the metal a useful real-time gauge of whether deleveraging pressure is returning. Higher US yields and a firmer USD/JPY show some haven demand unwinding, with the yen on the soft side in holiday-thinned trade. The Shanghai and Hong Kong open is the next test, given Beijing's new margin rules and the brokerages' talk of a bottom.

---

Wall Street's futures have found their feet after a brutal last week, but with Seoul still sliding and Tokyo away, this is a breather until proven otherwise.

Summary:

  • S&P 500 futures rose about 2.2% and Nasdaq 100 futures about 2.8% in early Asian trade, near session highs.
  • Spot gold rallied about 2.3% to around $3,620, and silver rose around 2.6%. Brent slipped to near $90 and WTI to around $83.
  • The dollar eased against most majors, with AUD/USD up about 0.4%, but USD/JPY rose to near 158.90.
  • The Kospi fell nearly 4% to around 4,680, with Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix sharply lower. Japan was closed, and China and Hong Kong had yet to open.
  • The US 10-year yield rose to about 4.95%.

US equity index futures bounced strongly in early Asian trade on Monday, a first sign of relief after Wall Street's worst week in years, though the rebound has yet to spread to Asian cash markets. By about 01:20 GMT (20:20 US Eastern on Sunday), S&P 500 futures were up around 2.2% near 7,090 and Nasdaq 100 futures had risen about 2.8% to around 25,830, trading close to their session highs.

The bounce follows a weekend of policy support and pushback. South Korea readied its market stabilisation fund and eased buyback rules, China cut margin requirements and trading fees, and US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned the Federal Reserve against overtightening. None of that changes the underlying concerns over AI valuations, but it has given short-term sellers a reason to pause.

Asia itself remains under pressure. Japanese markets are closed for a public holiday, and mainland China and Hong Kong had yet to open at the time of writing. In Seoul, the Kospi fell nearly 4% to around 4,680, extending Friday's slide despite the government's support package. Samsung Electronics was down about 4.6% and SK Hynix around 3.6% lower, and the Kosdaq lost close to 3%.

Gold rallied alongside stocks, a sign that last week's forced selling is easing for now. Spot gold rose about 2.3% to around $3,620 an ounce and silver gained around 2.6%. The move fits the pattern seen during the rout, when gold was sold to raise cash as equities fell, not bought as a haven. 

Oil edged lower, with Brent down around 0.3% near $90 a barrel and WTI around $83, as traders weighed lingering Gulf supply risks against forecasts of a surplus next year.

In currencies, the US dollar was softer against most majors. AUD/USD rose about 0.4% to around 0.6650, NZD/USD gained around 0.2%, and EUR/USD edged up to near 1.0980. The yen was the exception, with USD/JPY up about 0.2% to near 158.90 in holiday-thinned trade. The US 10-year Treasury yield rose around 4 basis points to about 4.95% as safe-haven demand eased.

For now this looks like a relief rally, not a turning point. The tone will be set by thin liquidity with Tokyo away, the open in Shanghai and Hong Kong, and whether US cash equities can hold the futures gains later on Monday. The Fed's December decision still looms over risk appetite.

item.title: Goldman sees European gas halving to €45 in 2027, but a cold winter could push it to €150
item.description:
A credible path to much cheaper gas would ease pressure on Europe's energy-intensive industries and utilities' input costs, and could weigh on gas futures further out the curve even while the winter contracts stay volatile. For oil, Goldman's surplus view gives bears a medium-term anchor. The near-term risks still point higher, though, while Gulf disruption continues, so dips may be shallow until flows clearly normalise. Lower energy import bills would remove one of the structural headwinds that has weighed on the euro. Rate differentials with a hiking Fed are likely to stay the dominant FX driver for now.

---

Last week:

  • Goldman sees Brent at $78 by end-2027 as oil surplus returns, flags near-term upside risk
  • Goldman Sachs gets bearish on oil prices but doesn't see help for consumers

---

Goldman sees Europe's gas bill roughly halving next year, but the forecast has to get through a winter first.

Summary:

  • Goldman Sachs forecasts European LNG prices averaging around €45/MWh in 2027, down from about €85 in mid-November. Its equity team sees TTF at around €31 by end-2027.
  • In oil, the bank sees Brent averaging $88 in 2027 and easing to $78 by December, as a surplus of about 2 million bpd builds.
  • Gulf exporters are adapting through new bypass pipelines, ship-to-ship transfers and naval escorts. LNG has adapted less well because it's harder to move.
  • In a cold winter with Gulf LNG exports at 25% to 30% of pre-war levels, gas could near €150 in the first quarter. Persistently weak exports would leave the 2027 average around €104.
  • The base case assumes no lasting Iran breakthrough and no damaging escalation.

European gas prices could roughly halve next year as Middle East energy supply adapts to disruption around the Strait of Hormuz, according to Goldman Sachs. That would offer potential relief for a region that has carried much of the cost of this year's energy shock. In research published on 18 November, the bank forecast European LNG prices averaging around €45 per megawatt hour in 2027, down from about €85 in mid-November.

The gas call comes with a broader view that the oil market has already moved into surplus. Goldman's base case has Brent averaging $88 a barrel in 2027 and easing to $78 by December, from around $93 in mid-November, as a surplus of about 2 million barrels per day builds. Gulf producers are increasingly working around Hormuz using new pipelines, ship-to-ship transfers and naval escorts, with roughly 3.8 million barrels per day of bypass pipeline capacity expected within a year. The bank's separate European equity outlook puts the TTF gas benchmark at around €31 by the end of 2027.

The bank was clear that the outlook for gas is far less certain than for oil. LNG is harder to reroute because it must be kept extremely cold and is more hazardous if attacked, so supply has adapted less effectively. Goldman said that if Gulf LNG exports run at only a quarter to 30% of pre-war levels this winter, and temperatures come in colder than normal, European prices could approach €150 in the first quarter of 2027. If Gulf exports stay low through next year, the 2027 average could be closer to €104. The base case assumes neither a lasting diplomatic breakthrough in the Iran war nor an escalation that causes long-term damage to energy infrastructure.

Goldman's research doesn't address currencies, but the implications for the euro are worth considering. Europe is a large net energy importer, so a sharp fall in gas and oil costs would improve its terms of trade and remove a significant drag on growth. That wouldn't guarantee a stronger euro, particularly with the Federal Reserve still raising rates, but it could make bearish views on the single currency harder to sustain through 2027.

The near-term test is the winter. A mild season and steady Gulf flows would support the base case, while a cold snap with tight LNG supply could push prices sharply higher before any relief arrives. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Chinese brokers see a bottom and a broader 2027 rally after Beijing's support push
item.description:
The brokers' calls point to two phases. Near term, rotation favours high-dividend defensives such as banks, insurers, utilities-style infrastructure and consumer staples like baijiu. In any rebound, beta should lead, through ChiNext growth names, small caps and technology. The combination of official support measures and upbeat state-linked research may limit downside in large caps in the near term. Without a pickup in leveraged and foreign inflows, though, rallies may struggle to stick. Moves in margin balances after 30 November and northbound flows will be the gauges to watch.

--- Beijing announced the support, and China's big brokers are now explaining how to trade it, which is familiar choreography in a market where policy and research tend to move together.

Summary:

  • CITIC Securities says the 22 November package targets the market's main pressures and signals a commitment to stability.
  • It sees valuation opportunities in quality leaders and expects a broader rally next year, favouring diversified exposure focused on sector leaders.
  • China Securities says high-dividend defensives still offer strong value while the market bottoms. It favours banks, white goods, baijiu, home textiles, insurers, railways and highways, telecoms, and shipping and ports.
  • It warns that dividend stocks could lag in a rebound, while small caps, tech, growth and thematic plays outperform.
  • Many large Chinese brokerages are state-controlled, and regulators have encouraged supportive behaviour in past downturns.

Main article: Two of China's biggest brokerages have struck a constructive tone on mainland stocks after regulators unveiled their latest package of market support measures. They offer investors a roadmap for positioning through what they describe as a bottoming phase.

CITIC Securities said the weekend measures target the main pressures on the market: overseas risks and volatility, net outflows of leveraged money and a sharp fall in ChiNext shares. The measures include lower margin financing requirements, plans for market-making on the ChiNext board and fee cuts. CITIC said easier margin rules would free up financing capacity and support liquidity, and market makers could draw in new capital and smooth swings on ChiNext. The broker said the package signals a commitment to stabilising the market, argued that the correction has been brought forward, and said high-quality leading companies now offer valuation opportunities. It expects any rally to broaden next year, making a diversified approach centred on sector leaders a viable strategy.

China Securities took a more defensive line for the near term. It said high-dividend sectors still offer strong allocation value while the market searches for a floor, noting that trading in these stocks has picked up without becoming crowded. It favours selected high-yield names with low institutional ownership, including banks, white goods makers, baijiu producers, home textiles, insurers, railways and highways, telecom operators, and shipping and ports. It cautioned, however, that if better external conditions, strong policy support and fresh inflows spark a rebound, dividend stocks could lag for a time while small caps, technology and growth shares, and thematic plays lead.

The upbeat commentary fits a familiar pattern. Many of China's largest brokerages are state-controlled, and in past periods of market stress regulators have encouraged financial institutions to support sentiment and avoid selling. Earlier this month the securities regulator urged fund managers to buy shares during the downturn. There is no indication these notes were directed, but readers may want to weigh research from state-linked firms alongside the policy push it echoes.

Whether the optimism holds depends on the same test facing the support measures themselves. If margin balances and turnover start to rise after the new rules take effect on 30 November, the brokers' call that the market is bottoming will look better founded. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6775 – Reuters estimate
item.description:
The People’s Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. 

---

Earlier:

  • China cuts margin requirement to 80% in fresh market support push, but will it work?

---

China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day’s closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point. A stronger-than-expected CNY midpoint is typically read as a sign the PBOC is leaning against depreciation pressure, while a weaker fixing for the CNY can indicate tolerance for a softer currency, often in response to dollar strength or domestic economic headwinds.In periods of heightened global volatility, such as shifts in US rate expectations, trade tensions or capital flow pressures, the fixing takes on added significance. For investors, it provides insight into Beijing’s currency priorities, balancing competitiveness, capital stability and financial market confidence.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: The AI winners may not exist yet, J.P. Morgan warns, as mega-IPOs flood the market
item.description:
J.P. Morgan's numbers push back on one popular explanation for the AI sell-off, that a flood of new shares is draining liquidity. That puts the focus back on valuations and earnings doubts as the real drivers. Strong household, foreign and buyback demand also suggests a deep pool of buyers if sentiment stabilises, which supports the buy-the-dip case. The point that much of the value creation now happens before listing is a caution for anyone chasing new AI listings, and it could weigh on post-IPO performance.

---

Earlier:

  • Goldman names 3 signals that could mark a bottom as the S&P 500 sits 12% below its record

---

The AI listing boom is huge in dollar terms but small next to the market absorbing it, and J.P. Morgan suggests the next big winners may still be private, or not yet born.

Summary:

  • J.P. Morgan Private Bank expects US IPO proceeds of around $290 billion in 2026, close to the 2021 peak of about $330 billion.
  • That is less than 1% of a roughly $70 trillion US stock market. SpaceX and Anthropic alone have raised more than $179 billion this year.
  • Demand is growing faster than supply: households bought more than $800 billion of equities in the first half, foreign investors over $350 billion, and buybacks have topped $1.3 trillion.
  • An estimated 85% to 95% of companies with more than $100 million in revenue remain private, and unicorns are worth about $8 trillion.
  • The bank warned that the eventual AI winners may not exist yet.

US companies are on course to raise around $290 billion through initial public offerings this year, close to the 2021 record of roughly $330 billion, according to J.P. Morgan Private Bank. The bank argues, though, that the wave of AI-driven listings is small relative to the size of the market. In a research piece published late last week, it said expected 2026 issuance amounts to less than 1% of a US stock market worth about $70 trillion, and described the supply as a drop in the bucket.

That makes this one of the strongest years for issuance in two decades, even before counting secondary offerings, SPACs or convertible notes. Mega-listings by companies such as SpaceX and Anthropic have together raised more than $179 billion this year.

The bank argued that demand is rising faster than supply. US households bought more than $800 billion of equities in the first half of 2026, international investors added over $350 billion, and corporate buybacks have topped $1.3 trillion so far this year. Net equity supply has turned positive for the first time since the 2020 to 2021 IPO boom, but J.P. Morgan said investor demand is growing more quickly.

It also suggested that today's listings play a different role from those of past decades. Many large companies used to list to raise money for years of future growth. Now they often list after much of their value has already been created in private markets. J.P. Morgan estimates that 85% to 95% of companies worldwide with more than $100 million in revenue remain private. It also estimates that unicorns, private start-ups valued at $1 billion or more, are together worth around $8 trillion. Plentiful private funding, including nearly $110 billion raised by US venture capital funds through the third quarter, lets companies delay listing.

The bank cautioned that the AI race is far from settled, saying "the eventual winners in AI may not even exist yet."

The timing stands out. The note came out as Wall Street suffered its worst week in years, with AI stocks at the centre of the sell-off and Anthropic's listing failing to revive risk appetite. J.P. Morgan's argument that the market can absorb new supply addresses one worry. It doesn't answer the bigger question now facing investors: whether the valuations being paid for AI growth can last. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: SNB's Martin eyes second-round effects after inflation jumps to 1.5%, hike in view
item.description:
Martin's focus on second-round effects is a hawkish signal, and it supports pricing for a December SNB hike. A tightening Swiss central bank alongside a hiking Fed changes the usual rate-differential story for the franc. Combined with strong safe-haven demand during the equity rout, that could keep the franc well bid, especially against the euro. That is the very currency risk Martin flagged, so the SNB may stay willing to lean against excessive franc strength even as it tightens. UBS shares remain exposed to headlines on the capital rules and any further talk of a headquarters move.

---

Swiss inflation is still within target, but its speed has the SNB watching wages and prices closely, and a December hike now looks like a live option.

Summary:

  • SNB Vice Chairman Antoine Martin told Le Matin Dimanche the bank is paying particular attention to possible second-round inflation effects.
  • Swiss annual inflation rose faster than expected to 1.5% in October from 1% in September, raising expectations of a December hike. The SNB targets 0% to 2%.
  • Chairman Martin Schlegel had said the jump surprised the bank.
  • Martin said the franc "very clearly" remains a safe haven and named exchange-rate swings as the SNB's main risk.
  • He reiterated SNB support for requiring UBS to fully capitalise its foreign subsidiaries and said any headquarters move would be for UBS management to decide.

The Swiss National Bank is closely watching for second-round effects from rising inflation, Vice Chairman Antoine Martin said in an interview published on Sunday, adding to expectations of a rate increase in December. Speaking to Swiss newspaper Le Matin Dimanche, Martin said inflation had continued to climb since the central bank's last policy decision and that policymakers were paying particular attention to possible second-round effects.

His remarks follow a sharper-than-expected jump in Swiss annual inflation to 1.5% in October from 1% in September, which raised market expectations of a hike at the SNB's next meeting. Chairman Martin Schlegel said after the data that the jump had caught the bank by surprise. Inflation is still inside the SNB's 0% to 2% target range, but it seems to be the speed of the increase, not its level, that concerns officials. Second-round effects, where higher prices lead to bigger wage demands and wider price increases, are what can turn a temporary shock into more lasting inflation.

Martin also defended the franc's status as a safe haven. He said it "very clearly" still plays that role and that, in real terms, it is close to where it traded against the euro five years ago. The currency weakened against the dollar and euro earlier in the year, then strengthened sharply in October as AI-related market turbulence, higher energy prices and concerns over French public debt drove demand for safety. He described exchange-rate swings between the franc, dollar and euro as the central bank's main risk.

On banking regulation, Martin repeated the SNB's support for a government proposal that would require UBS to fully capitalise its foreign subsidiaries. The proposal is part of the regulatory overhaul that followed the collapse of Credit Suisse in 2023. UBS has called the plan excessive and a threat to its competitiveness, fuelling speculation it could move its headquarters abroad. Martin said any such move would be for the bank's management to decide, while pointing to Switzerland's political stability, predictable legal framework and skilled workforce.

The next test is the December policy decision. How the SNB weighs fast-rising inflation against a franc that is again in demand will shape how far it is prepared to go. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

  • Spot gold fell about 2.7% on Friday to around $3,525 an ounce, a 14-month low, and lost roughly 9% over the week, its worst week in eight months.
  • The metal is now more than a third below its January record above $5,500.
  • ING's Ewa Manthey cited higher rate expectations and a firmer dollar, and said the equity rout may have prompted selling to raise cash.
  • Commerzbank's Carsten Fritsch pointed to renewed forced selling.
  • Goldman Sachs, after two forecast cuts this month, sees gold at $4,150 by end-2026 and $4,650 by end-2027.

Gold has lost its role as a refuge in the current market rout. Bank strategists point to forced selling and rising US rate expectations as the two forces behind its steepest weekly fall in eight months. Spot gold dropped about 2.7% on Friday to around $3,525 an ounce after touching a 14-month low. That left it down roughly 9% on the week and more than a third below its record above $5,500 in January.

ING commodities strategist Ewa Manthey said the macro backdrop had turned against the metal, with higher rate expectations and a firmer US dollar reducing its appeal. She added that the equity sell-off may also have pushed some investors to sell gold to raise cash. Commerzbank's Carsten Fritsch also pointed to renewed forced selling as a likely explanation for the latest leg lower.

That pattern is typical of a deleveraging phase. As losses build in leveraged equity positions, particularly in AI-linked stocks, investors sell what they can, not what they want to. Gold's deep liquidity makes it an easy source of cash. The metal kept falling last week even as Treasury yields eased and the dollar's momentum cooled, a sign that liquidation, not rates alone, was doing the damage. Silver fared worse, losing around 14% over the week.

Policy is the other weight. Futures price a December Federal Reserve rate hike as close to certain, and higher rates raise the cost of holding a metal that pays no yield. Goldman Sachs has trimmed its forecasts twice this month because of the Fed's hawkish shift. It sees gold at $4,150 by the end of 2026 and $4,650 by the end of 2027. It still expects a climb above $5,600 in 2028 as investor pressure eases and central bank buying continues.

For now, the outlook depends on the same forces driving stocks. Further equity losses could set off another round of margin-driven selling. Gold will probably need a sign that the Fed is ready to slow its tightening, or a steadier AI trade, before it can rebuild support.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Korea's market rescue fund is worth around $8 billion, but is 10.76 trillion won enough?
item.description:
The fund's size makes it more of a confidence signal than a market mover, so traders are likely to watch how quickly and how visibly it is deployed, not just its headline value. If it is activated and the selling doesn't slow, pressure could build for a larger fund or for the outright short-selling curbs that authorities have so far avoided. Heavy foreign short positioning also leaves room for sharp short-covering rallies if sentiment turns, which could make Kospi swings even wider in both directions this week. Any further weakness in Korean equities may also feed through to the won via foreign outflows.

---

Earlier:

  • Seoul readies a market fund unused since 2008 after the Kospi sinks
  • China cuts margin requirement to 80% in fresh market support push, but will it work?

---

Korea has dusted off an $8 billion backstop for a market that can trade several times that in a single day, so its real value may be the signal it sends.

Summary:

  • Korea's stock market stabilisation fund is worth 10.76 trillion won, around $8 billion, SBS reported. It is financed by financial institutions.
  • That matches the fund set up in 2020. If deployed, it would be the first use since 2008.
  • The package also eases buyback limits and launches a three-month crackdown on illegal short selling, but stops short of a short-selling ban.
  • Foreign investors made up nearly 80% of the roughly 5 trillion won of short-selling volume last week.
  • One strategist has argued that a fund below 25 trillion to 30 trillion won could be overwhelmed, with daily Kospi turnover often over 40 trillion won.

South Korea's stock market stabilisation fund, which the government is readying for immediate use, is worth 10.76 trillion won, or around $8 billion, Korean broadcaster SBS reported. The fund is financed by contributions from financial institutions and is designed to buy shares to cushion steep declines. If deployed, it would be the first time the tool has been used since the 2008 global financial crisis.

The figure matches the size of the fund set up during the pandemic market rout in 2020, which was established but never put to work. According to the Korea Times, Korea has created stabilisation funds five times: in 1990, 2003, 2008, 2020 and 2022.

Top economic officials announced on Sunday that preparations would start at once so the fund can be activated when needed. The package also eases daily share buyback limits for listed companies for three months and launches an intensive three-month crackdown on illegal short selling. It came after the Kospi slumped 5.2% on Friday to a 10-month low, leaving it nearly 47% below its June peak.

The size of the fund is likely to draw scrutiny. Daily turnover on the Kospi often exceeds 40 trillion won, almost four times the fund's firepower. Earlier this month, one strategist argued that anything below 25 trillion to 30 trillion won, roughly $19 billion to $22 billion, risked being overwhelmed by foreign institutional selling. That suggests the fund may work better as a signal of official intent than as a buyer big enough to turn the market on its own.

Authorities also stopped short of restricting short selling outright. SBS reported that foreign investors accounted for nearly 80%, or around 3.9 trillion won, of the roughly 5 trillion won of short-selling volume over the past week, and that this selling was seen as a key driver of the decline. The new monitoring targets only illegal activity.

The fund's real test will come if selling speeds up. Officials have framed it as a backstop, not an immediate buyer. The Bank of Korea's policy meeting on Thursday adds another source of pressure on an already fragile market, with economists expecting another 25 basis point hike. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Could Nvidia shareholders force Huang back? The 15% hurdle behind a long-shot idea
item.description:
For now this is a watch item, not a trading catalyst. There's no filing, no coalition and a board that has firmly closed the door. If it did escalate into a formal fight, the leadership uncertainty would likely weigh on Nvidia shares in the near term, whatever the outcome, at a time when AI stocks are already under heavy pressure. Some investors would treat a credible path back for Huang as positive for strategic continuity, which is why any SEC filings showing coordinated holders would draw immediate attention. The export compliance review is still the more important driver for the stock.

---

A shareholder revolt to bring Huang back makes a good headline, but with no filing, a 15% threshold and a board that has said no, it's one to watch, not one to bet on.

Summary:

  • Activist investor Bill Ackman says Huang's backers could seek a special shareholder meeting and that the threat of a vote might sway the board. He doesn't plan to get involved.
  • No formal campaign, filing or special meeting request has been reported.
  • Nvidia's bylaws require holders with 15% of voting power, held for a year, to call a special meeting. Huang owns about 3.6%.
  • Board chair Harvey Jones and interim CEO Colette Kress say the board won't reinstate Huang.
  • Pressure is coming from an open letter, some investors, President Trump and, as of Sunday, a softer stance from Treasury Secretary Bessent.

A shareholder route to bring Jensen Huang back to Nvidia is being floated, but for now it is an idea, not a campaign, and the hurdles are high. Activist investor Bill Ackman said at a Semafor conference last week that Huang's backers could try to force a special shareholder meeting. He argued that the threat of a vote alone might be enough to persuade the board to reinstate him, without the meeting ever taking place. Ackman said he was unlikely to get involved himself.

No formal action has been reported. There is no filing, no request for a special meeting and no named group of investors seeking to remove directors.

The numbers make it hard. Under bylaws adopted in 2024, shareholders can demand a special meeting only if together they have held at least 15% of the voting power for a full year. Huang's own stake was put at about 3.6% in Nvidia's May proxy, so his backers would need roughly another 11% from long-term holders. That is a large coalition for a company of Nvidia's size, and the one-year rule means no one can build a stake quickly. Even a successful vote to replace directors would not put a chief executive in place directly, because that decision belongs to the board.

The board has been clear. Chair Harvey Jones said on last week's earnings call that directors had unanimously accepted Huang's resignation and did not intend to reinstate him. Interim chief executive Colette Kress has since repeated that the board will not bring him back.

Public pressure is still building. An online open letter calling on the board to reinstate Huang while an independent investigation runs has drawn thousands of signatures, though most come from outside the company and the letter does not call for a vote. Some prominent investors have urged the board not to rush to replace him. President Donald Trump has said Huang should get his job back, and on Sunday Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent stopped ruling out a return.

For now, a boardroom challenge is a long shot. Prediction market traders price only around an 8% chance of Huang rejoining in a formal role by the end of 2026. The signals to watch are any regulatory filing showing investors coordinating, a formal meeting request, and the outcome of the export compliance review, which could change the board's thinking. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Bessent leaves door open to Huang return at Nvidia, a week after urging an outside CEO
item.description:
Removing Washington's apparent veto on Huang lowers one source of leadership uncertainty at the world's most important AI chipmaker, which could ease some of the pressure on Nvidia after last week's slide. The bigger regulatory overhang is still there, though. Any finding of export-control breaches could bring penalties or tighter limits on China-linked sales, which would hit revenue expectations directly. Traders are likely to treat the board's compliance response as a binary event for the stock and for AI sentiment more broadly. A clean answer would also strengthen the case for a Huang return.

---

Earlier:

  • US equity rout: Bessent cautions Fed against overtightening, before its December decision

--- A week ago Bessent wanted an outsider running Nvidia. Now the door is open for Huang, as long as the compliance answers hold up.

Summary:

  • On CBS on Sunday, Bessent declined to rule out Jensen Huang returning as Nvidia CEO, saying it depends on "where the buck stops."
  • On Fox News on 15 November, he had called for a shake-up and an outside successor, and gave Nvidia 10 days to answer compliance questions.
  • He said he assumed Huang didn't know a woman linked to the scandal was an alleged spy, and said his "culture of non-compliance" remark described a possibility.
  • He said the administration still lacks the answers it requested. Nvidia's CFO is running the company.
  • President Trump has said Huang should get his job back. Bessent did not directly address that.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has sharply softened his position on Jensen Huang. He declined to rule out the former chief executive's return to Nvidia, just a week after urging the chipmaker to look outside the company for his successor. Asked on CBS's Face the Nation on Sunday whether Huang should go back to running the company, Bessent said only that "we have to see where the buck stops." He also said he assumed Huang had not known that a woman at the centre of the scandal was an alleged spy.

That is a clear change from his appearance on Fox News on 15 November. That interview came three days after Huang stepped down following revelations about his personal relationships, including one with a woman US officials suspect of working for Chinese intelligence. On Fox, Bessent called for a dramatic shake-up at the top of Nvidia and said its next leader should come from outside. He questioned whether a culture of non-compliance had driven seemingly illicit chip sales to boost revenue and earnings, and gave the board and its outside counsel 10 days to provide answers.

On Sunday, Bessent dismissed the focus on Huang's relationship as something of a distraction from the compliance question. He stressed that his earlier remarks about a non-compliance culture described a possibility, not a finding. He also noted that Nvidia had dropped Megaspeed, the company at the centre of the export concerns, from its sales list in August 2025, though he said investigators still need to establish whether it acted as a pass-through.

The shift brings Bessent closer to President Donald Trump, who has said Huang should get his job back, although the Treasury Secretary did not directly address the president's view.

Bessent made clear that the investigation is not over. He said the administration still lacks the answers it requested, that officials have been in touch with Nvidia's interim management, lead directors and lawyers, and that the company should move quickly. Nvidia's chief financial officer is currently running the business.

With the 10-day window closing this week, the board's response on export compliance is now the main hurdle to any Huang return. It is also a key test for Nvidia shares after last week's AI-led market rout.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: China cuts margin requirement to 80% in fresh market support push, but will it work?
item.description:
The margin cut may help mainland sentiment at the open, especially in the high-beta growth names on ChiNext and the STAR board, where leveraged retail money tends to concentrate. Because the change only takes effect on 30 November, its direct flow impact is a week away, so traders may treat early gains as anticipatory and easy to reverse. Hong Kong-listed Chinese tech is outside the scope of the measures and stays more exposed to the global AI rout. The yuan is unlikely to react much unless the measures bring clear inflows back into mainland equities.

----

Earlier:

  • Seoul readies a market fund unused since 2008 after the Kospi sinks

---

Beijing is making it cheaper to borrow to buy stocks, but with margin balances already shrinking, the real shortage looks like confidence, not credit.

Summary:

  • China's three main exchanges will lower the minimum margin requirement for buying stocks on credit to 80% from 100%, effective 30 November, with CSRC approval.
  • The move reverses a January tightening and applies to both new and existing contracts.
  • Margin loans have fallen by more than 20% since late June, to about 2.2 trillion yuan. Chinese media estimate the change could free up close to 400 billion yuan.
  • The Shanghai and Shenzhen exchanges and the national clearing house announced fee cuts, and Shenzhen proposed market makers for ChiNext.
  • The steps follow a broader 2 November support package after mainland stocks' worst month in a decade.

China has rolled out a fresh round of stock market support, easing leverage rules and cutting trading costs in its latest attempt to steady share prices battered by the global sell-off in technology stocks. The Shanghai, Shenzhen and Beijing exchanges said on Sunday that, with approval from the China Securities Regulatory Commission, the minimum margin requirement for buying shares on credit will fall to 80% from 100%, effective 30 November. The lower ratio applies to existing as well as new margin contracts.

The move reverses a tightening introduced in January, when authorities were trying to cool the market, not revive it. The exchanges said margin financing had weakened and overall leverage was now low. According to Reuters, outstanding margin loans have fallen by more than a fifth since late June, to around 2.2 trillion yuan from about 3 trillion yuan. Chinese financial media estimated the change could, in theory, free up close to 400 billion yuan in extra buying power.

Alongside the margin change, the Shanghai and Shenzhen exchanges and the national clearing house, China Securities Depository and Clearing Corporation, announced a package of fee reductions. The Shenzhen exchange also published draft rules to introduce market makers on ChiNext, its growth-company board, aimed at smoothing price swings and improving liquidity.

Sunday's steps build on a larger package unveiled on 2 November, after mainland stocks had their worst monthly sell-off in a decade. That round included a third operation of the central bank's swap facility for brokers, funds and insurers, and a cheaper relending scheme for share buybacks that was made permanent. It also included a pledge by the securities regulator to optimise margin rules, which it has now delivered.

Whether the measures will work is far from certain. Easier margin rules lower the cost of borrowing to buy stocks, but they don't create demand on their own. Falling loan balances suggest investors have been choosing to cut risk, not being blocked from taking it. Higher leverage also cuts both ways: if prices keep falling, margin calls could force more selling and deepen the slide. The fee cuts are modest next to the scale of recent losses, and the ChiNext reform is still only a proposal.

The bigger test is outside China. Chinese tech shares have been caught in the same AI-driven rout that has hit Wall Street and Seoul, and domestic policy tools have limited power over global sentiment toward the sector. A steady rise in margin balances after 30 November would be the clearest sign that the support is drawing investors back in. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.
